latin.396: Alteram similitudinem ducis a toto naturali, corpore scilicet humano, eamque Thomae Aquinatis verbis exprimis: non, opinor, ut eius authoritate sententiam tuam fulcias, aut me commoveas; scis enim quam apud Ecclesias nostras sit nulla, sed quia eius verba tibi visa sunt commoda & dilucida. Ego autem qua mente dicta sint a Thoma utcunque intelligo, & quia intelligo, doctrinam continere a mente Ecclesiarum nostrarum diversam, non recipio: quo vero consilio a te sint recitata hoc loco non assequor, nisi forte idem prorsus sentias de peccato originali cum Thoma: quod de te suspicari non audeo. Ponit Thomas peccatum per carnis originem vitiatam ab Adamo in nos traduci, sive (ut habet in Summa) primum peccatum primi hominis originaliter transire in posteros; ac ostendit quomodo per semen ad animam rationalem perveniat. Sed concessa illa peccati traductione remanet dubitatio, quod defectus, qui ex vitiata origine trahuntur, non habeant rationem culpae; non enim merentur poenam, sed magis misericordiam, sicut Philosophus dicit de eo qui nascitur caecus, vel quocunque alio modo aliter orbatus. Et hoc ideo, quia de ratione culpae est quod sit voluntaria, & in potestate hominis cui culpa imputatur. Quaestio igitur erat, quomodo defectus illi, vel, ut loquitur in Summa, infectio, habeant rationem peccati, cum sint involuntarii in infantibus. Eius responsionem, quia a te laudatur, expendam per partes.
latin.397: Dicendum est, inquit, quod sicut peccatum actuale est peccatum personae, quod per voluntatem personae peccantis committitur; ita peccatum originale est peccatum naturae, quod per voluntatem principii humanae naturae commissum est. Distinguit duo peccata, unum actuale, alterum originale: illud personae, hoc naturae; illud per voluntatem personae peccantis, hoc per voluntatem principii naturae humanae commissum. Erantne igitur duae in Adamo voluntates, una personae, altera principii naturae humanae? Et, an peccatum per voluntatem principii naturae humanae fuit actuale, necne? Si voluit distinguere peccatum actuale Adami a corruptione habituali, quam in eius facultatibus reliquit, bona est doctrina, sed non bene expressa. Caeterum peccatum actuale Adami, si fuit personae, quomodo nobis imputatur? Sed pergamus. Est enim, inquit, considerandum, quod sicut diversa membra corporis partes sunt personae unius hominis, ita omnes homines sunt partes, & quasi quaedam membra humanae naturae: unde Porphyrius dicit, quod participatione speciei plures homines sunt unus homo.
latin.398: Diversa membra corporis sunt partes integrantes totius hominis. Omnes vero homines non sunt partes integrantes naturae humanae. Non componitur natura ex multis hominibus. Alioqui cum mihi natura humana insit integra, inessent mihi omnes homines. Sed sunt partes Logicae, sive subjectivae, ut vulgo loquuntur in scholis, & natura abstracta & praecisa ab individuis, ac universalitate donata totum est Logicum seu universale: sed hanc rationem totius non habet a parte rei, sed per mentis nostrae operationem. Itaque Metaphysice loquendo contra res habet. Persona est totum, natura pars: persona est id quod agit, natura id quo agit. Addit Thomas, videmus autem quod actus peccati exercitus per aliquod membrum, puta per manum, vel pedem, non habet rationem culpae ex voluntate manus vel pedis, sed ex voluntate totius hominis, a qua sicut a quodam principio derivatur motus peccati ad singula membra. Et similiter a voluntate Adae, qui fuit principium humanae naturae, tota inordinatio naturae habet culpae rationem in omnibus ad quos pervenit, quantum ad hoc quod susceptivi sunt culpae. Adverte quaeso quam non bene procedat ista similitudo.
latin.399: In praecedentibus verbis componebat naturam cum persona, omnes homines cum membris corporis. Unde oriebatur haec similitudo, ut se habet persona ad membra corporis, sic se habet natura ad omnes homines. Satis, ut innui, male: Non enim ut persona est principium quod actionis, membrum quo; sic natura est principium quod, homines principia quibus peccat. Sed contra, ut iam dixi. Iam autem quomodo istam comparationem ad institutum accommodat? Actus, inquit, peccati exercitus per aliquod membrum non habet rationem peccati ex voluntate illius membri, sed totius personae. Expectabam ut concluderet, ergo actus peccati exercitus per aliquem hominem non habet rationem peccati ex voluntate illius hominis, sed ex voluntate naturae humanae. Verum ille mutatis terminis, loco actus exerciti per homines aut hominem, posuit totam inordinationem naturae, & pro voluntate naturae humanae posuit voluntatem Adae qui fuit principium naturae humanae. Atqui primum accurate loquendo falsum est, Adam fuisse principium naturae humanae: Imo contra potius, natura humana fuit principium Adami. Est enim natura quodammodo pars suppositi: pars autem principium aliquomodo eius quod componit. Et, ut Logici loquuntur, natura humana prior est Adamo existendi consequentia. Est igitur Adamus principium seu causa, non absolute naturae humanae, sed naturae humanae quae in eius posteris fuit: quomodo pater quilibet principium est naturae posterorum, non suae. Deinde voluntas Adae tam eius personae voluntas fuit, quam mea meae; nec intelligo cur naturae voluntas dici debeat. Nam si Adamus principium fuit naturae humanae, inde non sequitur eius voluntatem fuisse voluntatem naturae, sequitur tantum Adamum fuisse principium voluntatis naturae humanae, aut certe naturam humanam non habere voluntatem, aut ad summum voluntatem Adami fuisse principium voluntatis naturae.
latin.400: Piget me diutius immorari in isto scholastico pulvere inanium subtilitatum, quibus tu me Thomae opera implicuisti, quem alioqui fabellis plurium rationum possem in suos autores dispellere, & dissipare: sed satis erit hoc loco duas huius similitudinis claudicationes observasse. Primum enim ideo actus per membrum aliquod corporis exercitus non habet rationem culpae ex voluntate illius membri, sed totius hominis, quia membro illi nulla est propria voluntas. At sua cuique homini propria est voluntas. Itaque membrum separatum nihil peccat, nihil agit. Homines singuli multa & agunt, & peccant separati ab Adamo, eorumque actiones peccata sunt, non quia proficiscuntur a voluntate Adami, sed quia, profectae a propria cuiusque voluntate, pugnant cum lege Dei. Deinde discere velim, cur haec comparatio locum habeat duntaxat respectu primi illius peccati actualis, non autem sequentium? desiitne simul ac peccavit Adamus, eius voluntas esse voluntas naturae, aut Adamus esse principium naturae humanae? Effecerit igitur ista comparatio, ut, non minus quam primum, reliqua Adami peccata nobis imputentur, contradicente Apostolo Rom. 5. Addam & tertiam claudicationem, idcirco actiones membrorum corporis rationem culpae habent ex voluntate totius hominis, quoniam membra corporis sunt voluntatis totius hominis organa, seu instrumenta, & eius imperio moventur; quo fit ut eorum actiones tribuantur voluntati personae ut causae principali, membris tantummodo ut causae instrumentali. Nos autem, opinor, organa non sumus Adami, nec movemur a voluntate Adami, nec ab eo imperantur actiones nostrae, nec, cum quis generat, id facit ut causa instrumentalis, Adami voluntati obsequens. Praeter hos omnes defectus quos memoravi, laborat alio vitio haec Thomae Aquinatis similitudo & ratiocinatio, eoque maximo. Non enim propositae difficultati ullo modo satisfacit. Urgere enim id possum, quod etiam doctissimus Chamierus adversus Pighium & Salmeronem urget. Eius verba ascribam: Cum peccatum dicitur esse voluntarium, intelligendum est de voluntate eius, cuius peccatum esse dicitur. At hoc certe sensu non potest dici in nobis peccatum illud Adami esse voluntarium, multo minus actus nostrae voluntatis. Neque enim est in nostra voluntate, neque a nostra voluntate: quia reipsa nostra voluntas nunquam fuit voluntas Adami. Si ergo nostrae voluntatis respectu voluntarium non est Adami peccatum, sed tantum respectu voluntatis Adami, certe nostrum peccatum non est, sed solius Adami.
latin.401: Tu quidem ais, voluntatem Adami, cum peccavit, fuisse voluntatem omnium hominum: sed affirmanti, nec rationem afferenti oppono Chamierum, voluntas nostra nunquam fuit voluntas Adami. Cum enim haec propositio sit negans, convertitur simpliciter in hanc, Voluntas Adami nunquam fuit voluntas nostra. Vin' tui huius dicti protraham in lucem absurditatem? 1. Si voluntas Adami fuit voluntas omnium hominum; igitur fuit voluntas universalis. Atqui constat tam singularem fuisse, quam alius cuiusvis. 2. Si voluntas Adami fuit, exempli causa, mea voluntas, igitur etiam eius anima fuit mea anima, & eius corpus fuit meum corpus, & eius os fuit meum os, & eius uxor fuit mea uxor &c. 3. Si voluntas Adami fuit mea voluntas, igitur duas habeo voluntates, unam aliquot millibus annorum antequam essem; alteram creatam nuper, annis abhinc fere quinquaginta, alteram ab altera realiter, immo localiter, divisam & separatam, unam communem, alteram propriam. Porro si duas voluntates habeo, etiam duas animas, duo corpora. Itaque qui me unum hominem esse putabam, evasi in duos, unum communem, alterum proprium; illum pridem fato suo functum, hunc adhuc viventem. Noli confugere ad figuras sermonis. Vis enim nobis omnibus vere & proprie imputari peccatum Adami, ac proinde nos illud vere & proprie commisisse. Non commisimus autem vere & proprie, nisi voluntas Adami qua commissum est vere & proprie nostra fuerit voluntas. 4. Si voluntas Adami fuit voluntas omnium hominum, igitur actus voluntatis Adami fuerunt actus omnium hominum: idem dicendum de actibus mentis. Quod si actus voluntatis eius eliciti fuerunt actus omnium hominum, etiam proculdubio actus eius voluntatis imperati. Cum loquebatur, loquebantur omnes homines; cum ambulabat, ambulabant omnes; cum edebat, edebant omnes; cum gignebat, gignebant omnes. Hoccine tibi probatur? nisi fortasse vis hoc privilegium habuisse voluntatem Adami ut nostra esset voluntas, pro eo duntaxat momento quo peccavit: mallem fuisset alio potius tempore.

pass_a.396: Placeus opens the second likeness: Thomas's human-body whole, cited not for authority (null among our Churches) but for handy clarity. He understands Thomas's mind as diverse from our Churches and does not receive it; he cannot see why it is recited unless the opponent thinks with Thomas on original sin—which he will not suspect. Thomas: sin traduced via vitiated fleshly origin / first sin passes originally into posterity through seed to the rational soul. Granting traduction, defects from vitiated origin lack fault's nature (they merit mercy, as of one born blind), because fault must be voluntary and in the man's power. So how can infection in infants be sin when involuntary? Placeus will weigh Thomas's praised reply part by part.
pass_a.397: Thomas: actual sin is the person's via the sinning person's will; original sin is nature's via the will of human nature's principle. Placeus asks: two wills in Adam—person and nature-principle? Was the nature-principle sin actual? Distinguishing actual sin from habitual corruption left in faculties may be good doctrine, badly expressed; but if actual sin was of the person, how is it imputed to us? Thomas continues: as diverse members are parts of one person's body, all men are parts/members of human nature—Porphyry: by species-participation many men are one man.
pass_a.398: Placeus: bodily members integrate the whole man; men do not integrate human nature—nature is not composed of many men, else all men would be in me. They are only logical/subjective parts; a universal whole exists by the mind's operation, not from the thing. Metaphysically person is whole and nature part—person what acts, nature by which. Thomas: sin through hand or foot has fault from the whole man's will, not the member's; likewise from Adam as principle of human nature the whole inordination has fault in all capable of it. Placeus: mark how badly this likeness proceeds.
pass_a.399: Thomas aligned nature with person and all men with bodily members—as person stands to members, so nature to all men. Placeus: badly enough; the quod/quo roles reverse—it is not that nature is the principle-which and men the principles-by-which it sins. Expected conclusion from the hand/foot premise: sin through a man has fault from human nature's will, not that man's. Thomas swapped terms—put the whole inordination of nature and Adam's will as nature's principle. But accurately Adam is not absolutely human nature's principle; rather nature is somehow a part of the supposit and prior to Adam in existing, and Adam is cause only of the human nature in his posterity, as any father of his posterity's nature, not his own. Adam's will was his person's will as mine is mine; calling it nature's will does not follow from his being principle of nature—at most he is principle of nature's will, or human nature has no will, or his will was principle of nature's will.
pass_a.400: Placeus tires of lingering in scholastic dust of empty subtleties and notes two limps of the likeness: (1) a member has no proper will of its own, but each man does—so separated men do and sin many things from their own wills against God's law, not because they proceed from Adam's will; (2) why does the comparison hold only for that first actual sin, not later ones—did Adam's will cease to be nature's will, or Adam to be human nature's principle, the moment he sinned? Then later sins would be imputed no less, against the Apostle in Rom. 5. Third limp: members' actions have fault from the whole man's will because they are organs or instruments moved by his command; we are not Adam's organs, nor moved or commanded by his will, nor instrumental causes in generation obeying him. Greatest vice: the likeness in no way satisfies the difficulty proposed. Chamier against Pighius and Salmeron: when sin is called voluntary it means of his will whose sin it is said to be; Adam's sin cannot be voluntary in us, much less our act of will, because our will never was Adam's—so if not voluntary respecting our will it is Adam's sin alone.
pass_a.401: Opponent affirms Adam's will when he sinned was the will of all men without bringing a reason. Placeus with Chamier: our will never was Adam's will, which converts simply to Adam's will never was ours. Shall the absurdity be dragged into light? (1) Then it was a universal will—yet Adam's was as singular as anyone else's. (2) If his will was mine, his soul, body, mouth, and wife were mine too. (3) Then I have two wills—one thousands of years before I was, another created nearly fifty years ago—really and locally divided, one common and one proper; so also two souls and bodies, and I who thought myself one man become two—one common long dead, one proper still living. Figures of speech will not save wanting true proper imputation without Adam's will truly and properly ours. (4) Elicited and commanded acts of will and mind would be all men's—when he spoke, walked, ate, begot, all did. Does that please—unless the privilege of being our will holds only for the moment of the sin? Better another time. Tip before GAR's Augustine reply.

396: You draw a second likeness from a natural whole—namely the human body—and express it in Thomas Aquinas's words: not, I think, to prop your sentence by his authority or to move me (you know how null that is among our Churches), but because his words seemed handy and clear to you. I understand somehow in what mind Thomas spoke them, and because I understand that they contain a doctrine diverse from our Churches' mind, I do not receive them; and I do not see with what counsel you recited them here, unless you happen to think exactly with Thomas on original sin—which I dare not suspect of you. Thomas holds that sin is traduced into us from Adam through vitiated fleshly origin, or (as in the Summa) that the first man's first sin passes originally into posterity; and he shows how it reaches the rational soul through seed. But granting that traduction of sin, the doubt remains that defects drawn from a vitiated origin do not have the nature of fault; for they do not merit penalty but rather mercy, as the Philosopher says of one born blind or otherwise bereft. And that is because it belongs to fault's nature to be voluntary and in the power of the man to whom fault is imputed. The question, then, was how those defects—or, as the Summa says, the infection—have the nature of sin when they are involuntary in infants. His reply, since you praise it, I will weigh part by part.
397: It must be said, he says, that just as actual sin is a person's sin, committed through the will of the sinning person, so original sin is nature's sin, committed through the will of the principle of human nature. He distinguishes two sins, one actual, the other original: that of the person, this of nature; that through the sinning person's will, this through the will of human nature's principle. Were there then two wills in Adam—one of the person, another of human nature's principle? And was the sin through the principle's will actual, or not? If he meant to distinguish Adam's actual sin from the habitual corruption left in his faculties, the doctrine is good, but not well expressed. But if Adam's actual sin was of the person, how is it imputed to us? Yet let us go on. For it is to be considered, he says, that just as the body's diverse members are parts of one man's person, so all men are parts and as it were certain members of human nature: whence Porphyry says that by participation in the species many men are one man.
398: The body's diverse members are integrating parts of the whole man. But all men are not integrating parts of human nature. Nature is not composed of many men. Otherwise, since human nature is in me entire, all men would be in me. They are Logical or subjective parts, as the schools say, and nature abstracted and cut off from individuals and given universality is a Logical or universal whole—but it has that reason of a whole not from the side of the thing, but through our mind's operation. So Metaphysically speaking the matter is the contrary. Person is the whole, nature the part: person is what acts, nature that by which it acts. Thomas adds: we see that an act of sin exercised through some member—say hand or foot—has the nature of fault not from the hand's or foot's will but from the whole man's will, from which as from a principle the motion of sin is derived to the several members. And likewise from Adam's will, who was the principle of human nature, the whole inordination of nature has the nature of fault in all to whom it reaches, insofar as they are capable of fault. Mark, I pray, how badly this likeness proceeds.
399: In the preceding words he was composing nature with person, all men with the body's members. Whence arose this likeness: as person stands to the body's members, so nature stands to all men. Badly enough, as I hinted: for it is not that as person is the principle-which of the action and the member the principle-by-which, so nature is the principle-which and men the principles-by-which it sins. Rather the contrary, as I already said. Now how does he fit that comparison to the point? An act of sin exercised through some member, he says, has the nature of sin not from that member's will but from the whole person's. I expected him to conclude: therefore an act of sin exercised through some man has the nature of sin not from that man's will but from human nature's will. But he, changing terms, put in place of an act exercised through men or a man the whole inordination of nature, and in place of human nature's will put Adam's will who was the principle of human nature. Yet first, accurately speaking, it is false that Adam was the principle of human nature: rather, on the contrary, human nature was Adam's principle. For nature is somehow a part of the supposit; and a part is somehow a principle of what it composes. And as the Logicians say, human nature is prior to Adam in the consequence of existing. Therefore Adam is principle or cause not of human nature absolutely, but of the human nature that was in his posterity—as any father is principle of his posterity's nature, not of his own. Next, Adam's will was his person's will as mine is mine; nor do I understand why it should be called nature's will. For if Adam was principle of human nature, it does not follow that his will was nature's will—only that Adam was principle of human nature's will, or that human nature has no will, or at most that Adam's will was the principle of nature's will.
400: It irks me to linger longer in that scholastic dust of empty subtleties with which you have entangled me by Thomas's work—whom otherwise I could scatter back to his authors with the little stories of many reasons: but it will be enough here to have noted two limps of this likeness. First: an act exercised through some bodily member has the nature of fault from the whole man's will, not that member's, because that member has no proper will of its own. But each man has his own proper will. So a separated member sins nothing, does nothing. Individual men do and sin many things separated from Adam, and their actions are sins not because they proceed from Adam's will, but because, proceeding from each one's own will, they clash with God's law. Next I would learn why this comparison holds only respecting that first actual sin, not the following ones: did Adam's will cease to be nature's will, or Adam to be human nature's principle, the moment he sinned? Then this comparison would make Adam's later sins no less imputed to us than the first—contradicting the Apostle, Rom. 5. I add a third limp: members' actions have fault from the whole man's will because the body's members are organs or instruments of the whole man's will and are moved by his command; so their actions are ascribed to the person's will as principal cause, to the members only as instrumental. But we, I think, are not Adam's organs, nor are we moved by Adam's will, nor are our actions commanded by him, nor when someone generates does he do it as an instrumental cause obeying Adam's will. Besides all these defects I have mentioned, this likeness and reasoning of Thomas Aquinas labors under another and greatest vice. For it in no way satisfies the difficulty proposed. I can press what the most learned Chamier also presses against Pighius and Salmeron. I will copy his words: When sin is said to be voluntary, it is to be understood of the will of him whose sin it is said to be. But in that sense Adam's sin cannot be said to be voluntary in us, much less an act of our will. For it is neither in our will nor from our will: because in very deed our will never was Adam's will. If therefore Adam's sin is not voluntary with respect to our will, but only with respect to Adam's will, certainly it is not our sin, but Adam's alone.
401: You indeed say that Adam's will, when he sinned, was the will of all men: but to one who affirms without bringing a reason I oppose Chamier—our will never was Adam's will. And since that proposition is negative, it converts simply into this: Adam's will never was our will. Shall I drag the absurdity of your saying into the light? 1. If Adam's will was the will of all men, then it was a universal will. Yet it is clear it was as singular as anyone else's. 2. If Adam's will was, for example, my will, then also his soul was my soul, and his body my body, and his mouth my mouth, and his wife my wife, &c. 3. If Adam's will was my will, then I have two wills—one some thousands of years before I was; another created lately, nearly fifty years ago—one really, even locally, divided and separated from the other, one common, one proper. Further, if I have two wills, also two souls, two bodies. So I who thought myself one man have turned out two—one common, one proper; that one long since dead, this one still living. Do not flee to figures of speech. For you want Adam's sin truly and properly imputed to us all, and so us to have truly and properly committed it. But we did not truly and properly commit it unless Adam's will by which it was committed was truly and properly our will. 4. If Adam's will was the will of all men, then Adam's acts of will were acts of all men—the same of acts of mind. And if his elicited acts of will were acts of all men, then doubtless also his commanded acts of will. When he spoke, all men spoke; when he walked, all walked; when he ate, all ate; when he begot, all begot. Does this please you?—unless perhaps you want Adam's will to have had this privilege of being ours only for that moment when he sinned: I would rather it had been at some other time.
